problem.title: Hosting an open-source monorepo
problem.context: An open-source foundation hosts a 12-year, 40 GB monorepo with about 300 daily pushes and 2,000 contributors across five continents. Most clones come from CI and first-time contributors who need only the latest version. Four volunteers operate donated servers in Europe and North America.

requirements.text: Accept pushes from the maintainers to a single canonical repository over the standard Git protocol.
Let a first-time contributor start working without downloading the whole history.
A contributor in Asia or South America clones the latest version within two minutes on a 50 Mbit/s connection.
A CI job that starts after a push has been accepted always fetches that push.
Four volunteers run the service in their spare time.

points.description: The servers’ local plain Git repositories are authoritative, with each update coordinated as a three-phase transaction and replicated to three copies, succeeding after a majority records it. Clients use partial clone and sparse checkout, while fetches and checkouts are routed to the nearest replica containing the latest state. Trade-off: This provides durable copies, atomic reference updates, reduced client transfer, and potentially lower read latency. It gives up simpler operations and write latency because replicas must coordinate, and requires careful replica freshness tracking; partial clones also complicate clients and may require later object retrieval.

The object-storage append-only log is authoritative for objects and references, with writers using compare-and-swap when appending reference updates. Stateless servers reconstruct repositories into local caches from the log and serve reads, while Git partial clone and sparse checkout limit client transfers. Trade-off: This provides durable storage, machine-loss tolerance, interchangeable read servers, and reduced client downloads. It gives up fast independent serving when log access or cache rebuilding is slow and relies on object-storage CAS semantics rather than consensus for concurrent updates.

A file server holds each plain Git repository as the authoritative copy and serializes all reference updates. Regional cache servers serve read traffic, while clients use a virtual filesystem that fetches needed objects on demand, forwarding cache misses to the file-server origin. Trade-off: This is simple and provides centralized update ordering, nearby reads, and reduced client downloads. It sacrifices durability and availability through its single repository copy and server, and concentrates writes at one server.

Servers keep plain Git repositories as the authoritative state, maintaining three replicas and coordinating reference updates through a three-phase transaction. Developers use partial clone and sparse checkout, while regional cache servers serve nearby fetches and clones, forwarding misses to an origin. Trade-off: This combines durable majority replication, atomic reference coordination, reduced client transfer, and lower-latency reads. It adds replica-coordination and recovery complexity, while caches may require careful invalidation or consistency handling after updates.

The object-storage append-only log is the authoritative repository state, with reference updates committed by compare-and-swap; servers reconstruct local cached copies from it and serve reads without holding unique data. Developers use a virtual filesystem that fetches objects on demand, while any server can rebuild or warm its cache as needed. Trade-off: This gains durable centralized storage, stateless failover, and reduced client downloads, but log replay, cache misses, and object-fetch latency can slow reads. The virtual filesystem also adds client and filesystem complexity and depends on timely object retrieval.

approaches.idea: What if local plain Git repositories use replicated majority writes and transactionally coordinated references, with regional reads?
What if an object-storage log is authoritative and stateless servers derive read caches from it?
What if one file server keeps the only copy, while regional caches and on-demand client objects reduce read work?
approaches.dropped_because: A single repository copy sacrifices durability and availability across two donated data-centre sites.

approaches.idea: What if the log-backed approach uses on-demand virtualized client objects to reduce initial transfer further?

trajectory.hypothesis: Replicated Git state and coordinated ref updates should serve R1 and Q2; partial clone should serve R2 and partly serve Q1.

tradeoffs.note: Majority replication and multi-replica transactions strengthen durable, ordered writes but add operational work for a small volunteer team.
Partial transfer reduces the initial checkout but the space supplies no two-minute performance result.

trajectory.observation: The point has no source attesting the complete combination. The nearest up-to-date replica directly supports freshness, while the space gives no measured clone time or operational staffing estimate.

trajectory.hypothesis: The durable log and CAS should serve R1 and partly Q2; partial transfer and local caches should serve R2 and partly Q1.

tradeoffs.note: A canonical log simplifies the authority model, but the space does not establish that a CI read always observes an accepted append.
Partial transfer and local caches cut likely data movement, but neither gives a quantified two-minute result.
The log and rebuildable caches avoid unique server state but add components and recovery behavior for volunteers to operate.

trajectory.observation: Git at any scale attests this complete design point. Its log CAS ordering is promising for accepted pushes, but the evidence does not quantify the CI read guarantee.

trajectory.hypothesis: A single serialized origin should keep pushes simple; caches and on-demand objects should serve R2 and partly serve Q1.

tradeoffs.note: One copy is easier to operate but a machine or site loss can make accepted state unavailable, so read-after-push is not assured.
On-demand objects and regional caches reduce initial downloads but add client and cache behavior, with no measured clone time.

trajectory.observation: This is operationally simple, but its single-copy durability choice is a poor fit for a service split across two data centres and undermines reliable CI access after accepted pushes.

trajectory.hypothesis: Replacing nearest-replica routing with regional caches should improve Q1 while keeping partial transfer and explicit replica coordination for Q2.

tradeoffs.note: Replicated transactional writes support an authoritative accepted push but require volunteers to maintain coordination and recovery.
Sparse transfer and regional caches reduce client data movement, but cache freshness and the numerical deadline remain unproven.

trajectory.observation: Regional caches plausibly reduce distance for contributors, but add a freshness path that weakens the direct post-push guarantee compared with routing to a known up-to-date replica. Q1 remains unproven without measurements.

trajectory.hypothesis: On-demand objects should reduce the initial transfer beyond partial clone for R2 and Q1 while retaining the log and rebuildable read servers.

tradeoffs.note: A canonical log and CAS make one ordered write authority, but immediate CI visibility is not guaranteed by the design-space evidence.
Fetching objects on demand limits initial downloads, but adds virtual filesystem support and remote object latency to the clone path and operational surface.

trajectory.observation: Git at any scale attests the combination. The lower initial transfer is attractive, but the source evidence is mixed for virtualized filesystems and does not establish the target clone time; this does not beat the partial-clone point overall.

alternatives.name: Replicated Git with regional reads
alternatives.summary: Keep plain Git repositories authoritative, coordinate updates across three replicas, and serve nearby reads from regional caches. Use partial clone with sparse checkout for contributor and CI transfers.

choices.reason: Plain Git repository state gives maintainers a canonical repository using standard Git.
Majority replication preserves accepted writes across copies.
Transactional ref updates coordinate concurrent replica state.
Fetch only needed history and files to reduce first-checkout transfer.
Regional caches place reads nearer to contributors.

considered.reason: A nearest known up-to-date replica makes freshness more direct but offers less regional cache reuse.

relations.note: Replication is chosen after selecting local Git repositories as authority.
The regional read cache is compatible with replicated Git repositories.
Reference coordination follows the repository authority decision.
Partial clone is paired with regional read caches.

alternatives.name: Object-storage log with partial clones
alternatives.summary: Make the append-only object-storage log authoritative, use CAS for reference updates, and rebuild stateless local read caches. Partial clone limits client transfer.

choices.reason: The log is a single canonical authority from which plain Git serving state is derived.
Object storage retains durable log data while serving machines remain replaceable.
Compare-and-swap orders writes to the authoritative log.
Partial clone transfers only the requested history and files.
Stateless servers can rebuild local copies from the log and serve read traffic.

considered.reason: On-demand objects may cut initial transfer further, but add client complexity and have mixed source support.

relations.note: Object-storage durability follows choosing the log as authority.
Rebuildable stateless servers fit durability delegated to object storage.
CAS applies to the selected authoritative log.
Partial clone works with stateless read servers.

adrs.title: Repository authority, durability, and accepted writes
adrs.context: Maintainers need one canonical repository over standard Git, and CI must observe every accepted push. Local replicated Git offers explicit transactional coordination; an object-storage log provides one durable write authority with CAS, while server caches are derived. Neither combination has measured proof of the exact CI guarantee in this problem.

options.name: Replicated plain Git
pros: Canonical state remains in plain Git repositories.
Three replicas and coordinated reference transactions support durable accepted updates.
cons: Replica coordination and recovery add volunteer operations work.
The space does not establish the exact CI visibility guarantee.
options.reason: A1 favors direct Git authority and explicit replica coordination for pushes.

options.name: Object-storage log authority
pros: One append-only authority gives derived servers no unique state.
CAS sequences reference updates without coordinating Git replicas.
cons: Correct immediate read visibility depends on log and cache behavior not quantified here.
Adds an object-storage log and reconstruction path.
options.reason: B1 favors durable centralized authority and replaceable serving nodes.

options.name: Single file-server copy
cons: A single copy risks availability and loss across donated sites.
options.reason: Dropped because it gives up durability and can leave CI unable to fetch accepted state.

adrs.title: Contributor transfer and read serving
adrs.context: New contributors and CI need small, fast checkouts across continents, while CI reads must remain fresh after a push. Partial clone is a standard Git transfer option; on-demand virtual filesystems can defer more object transfer but bring mixed support. Regional caches favor proximity, whereas nearest-up-to-date reads prioritize freshness and log-derived caches favor interchangeable servers.

options.name: Partial clone with nearby cache reads
pros: Partial transfer serves first-time contributors without full history.
Regional cache servers put reads closer to distant contributors.
cons: Cache freshness can complicate post-push reads.
No measured data proves the two-minute target.
options.reason: A1 chooses lower geographic read distance while retaining standard Git partial clone.

options.name: Partial clone with stateless read servers
pros: Partial clone limits client data transfer.
Servers can rebuild local cached copies from durable log state.
cons: Cache misses and rebuilds can add latency.
No measured data proves the two-minute target or immediate post-push fetch behavior.
options.reason: B1 keeps client transfer modest and pairs reads with replaceable log-derived servers.

options.name: Virtualized client with regional caches
pros: Objects transfer on demand and regional caches reduce distance.
cons: Virtual filesystem support is mixed and cache freshness is not assured.
options.reason: Set aside because it increases client complexity without measured evidence for Q1.

options.name: Virtualized client with stateless servers
pros: On-demand objects reduce initial client transfer and servers remain replaceable.
cons: Object retrieval and cache rebuild latency can hurt the deadline; client and operations complexity increases.
options.reason: The exploration did not improve on the partial-clone alternative for this volunteer-run service.

unaddressed.note: The space has no dimension for operator workload, staffing, or spare-time maintenance burden.
